update-your-paperwork-after-a-life-chang.title: What to update after a major life change
update-your-paperwork-after-a-life-chang.dek: After marriage, divorce, a move, a new child or job, check real deadlines first, then update contacts, coverage and the names on important forms.
update-your-paperwork-after-a-life-chang.metaDescription: After marriage, divorce, a move, a new child or job, check real deadlines first, then update contacts, coverage and the names on important forms.

paragraphs: After a major life change, check time-sensitive coverage and legal obligations first, then review beneficiaries, decision makers, contact details and document locations. Do not assume one notification updates every organization, or that every health plan gives you 60 days. Build a list by institution and confirm each deadline directly.

A new baby or move creates urgent everyday work before the paperwork even becomes visible. The useful task is not to rewrite every document tonight. It is to identify which arrangements the event actually changes, which have a clock and which need professional advice. This guide uses US examples and does not determine your tax, insurance or estate position.

body.heading: Start with the event
rows: Health enrollment, names if changing, beneficiaries and medical contacts.
A new spouse automatically replaces every old designation.
Coverage loss, court orders, account permissions and decision makers.
You can freely change every asset or beneficiary during proceedings.
Dependent enrollment, care planning and beneficiary arrangements.
Every plan has the same enrollment window.
Insurance location, official address updates, school or vehicle duties.
Forwarded mail updates the underlying record.
Coverage dates, new benefits and old plan contacts.
A former plan or policy follows you automatically.
Contact, agent and beneficiary arrangements using that name.
A backup exists on every form.

body.heading: Make the update list actionable
items: Write the event and actual date, then identify any notices or agreements already received. Keep them together.
Contact the health plan or benefits administrator promptly. Ask the exact enrollment deadline, documents, effective date and submission method.
Review beneficiaries and ownership arrangements account by account. Check restrictions and required consents before requesting changes.
Review emergency contacts, health care agents, financial helpers, caregivers and backups. Ask whether the people named remain willing and able.
Update names or addresses through each institution's official process, retaining required identity evidence and confirmation.
Record requested, submitted and confirmed separately. Replace obsolete handoff pages once the underlying arrangement is actually changed.

paragraphs: [Open the free life-change paperwork and deadline tracker](/guides/print/library/update-your-paperwork-after-a-life-change.html). Use the worksheet without an account or purchase.

body.alt: Three separate deadline checks distinguish employer coverage, Marketplace coverage and other life-change paperwork.
body.caption: Do not apply a 60-day Marketplace window to every health plan.

body.heading: The health-coverage clocks differ
paragraphs: The [Department of Labor](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/ebsa/about-ebsa/our-activities/resource-center/publications/life-changes-require-health-choices) describes job-based special enrollment requests generally within 30 days of marriage or a new child. [HealthCare.gov](https://www.healthcare.gov/coverage-outside-open-enrollment/special-enrollment-period/) describes Marketplace household-event windows commonly based on the past 60 days, with event-specific conditions. These are not interchangeable clocks.

For example, divorce without loss of coverage does not by itself create the Marketplace special enrollment opportunity described on that page. Ask which event and coverage arrangement apply. Confirm the deadline with the actual plan and act promptly rather than waiting until the longest window you found online.

body.heading: Example: one new child, several separate updates
paragraphs: Invented example: an employee welcomes a child and makes three entries: dependent enrollment with the employer plan, emergency contact updates, and a legal-planning appointment about guardianship and beneficiaries. The employee contacts the benefits administrator immediately, obtains the applicable deadline and submits through the required channel.

The family does not assume the hospital notified the employer or that a payroll update added insurance. The tracker retains submission confirmation and a later coverage confirmation. A discussion of who would care for the child is recorded as planning in progress until the relevant legal documents are completed correctly.

body.heading: Beneficiary review is not a blanket legal conclusion
paragraphs: Review each retirement plan, life policy and payable-on-death arrangement directly. Ask who is currently named, whether a contingent beneficiary exists, and what consent, court order or plan restriction applies. Do not assume a will alone changes a designation or that marriage and divorce have identical effects across all accounts.

A new spouse may have rights under some plans, while divorce-related changes may be constrained by law, plan terms or orders. If any of that is unclear, ask the plan administrator and a qualified adviser. The organizing action is to obtain the current record, not to predict who would legally receive the money.

body.alt: Four update stages separate reviewing, submitting, confirming and replacing an outdated personal record.
body.caption: Track the underlying change before marking your own list complete.

body.heading: Get a precise answer

items.line: This life event happened on this date. What enrollment opportunity applies to this plan, what is the final submission date, and how do I confirm the effective coverage date?
Please confirm the current primary and contingent beneficiaries and any consent, court-order or plan restrictions on changes. What evidence will show that an accepted change is effective?

body.heading: Identity and address changes need their own evidence
paragraphs: A legal name change is different from choosing to use a new name socially. Follow each agency's current documentary process and check dependencies before sending scarce originals. Avoid a universal instruction about which office must always be first; the correct sequence can depend on the document, jurisdiction and name-change basis.

For a move, review property and vehicle insurance before assuming the old policy covers the new circumstances. Update official records individually and identify local deadlines from the responsible authority. Mail forwarding is helpful but is not proof that an insurer, licensing agency or benefit program has recorded your new details.

body.heading: When to stop and seek advice
paragraphs: Get qualified advice before acting where there is a separation dispute, protective order, contested ownership, trust, pension division, cross-border move or uncertain tax consequence. Do not cancel coverage or remove someone from an account simply because a general checklist says to review it. Review means establish the facts before making a permitted change.

If a deadline may already have passed, contact the plan or institution promptly and ask what options remain. Keep the response and any appeal instructions. Do not backdate an application or assume the next open enrollment is the only possible route without checking.

body.heading: Finish with the handoff record
paragraphs: Once the provider confirms a change, update the emergency file, bill list or document-location index that points to it. Keep the event date and confirmation date distinct. A spreadsheet saying "changed" is weak evidence if the underlying form was only drafted.

Schedule another look when the next related event occurs or a pending response is due. The goal is not a permanently completed binder. It is a clear record of what is current, what was submitted and what still needs an answer.

items.q: Do I always have 60 days to add a baby to insurance?
items.a: No. Marketplace and employer-plan rules differ. Department of Labor guidance describes job-based requests generally within 30 days, while HealthCare.gov describes a 60-day opportunity for certain household events. Contact the actual plan promptly and obtain the deadline and effective-date rules for your situation.

items.q: Does divorce automatically remove my ex from beneficiary forms?
items.a: Do not assume either automatic removal or automatic retention for every asset. The result can depend on law, plan terms and court orders. Obtain current designations and restrictions directly, then seek advice before changing anything affected by the divorce. A general checklist cannot resolve the legal effect of an individual designation.

items.q: What proves an update is finished?
items.a: Keep the accepted submission and the institution's confirmation of the effective change. A saved draft, mailed envelope or pending request does not necessarily prove the record changed. Update your own handoff page only with the actual status, and follow up if the provider's confirmation is missing or inconsistent.

sources.name: Department of Labor: life changes and health choices
sources.note: Official article text returned through search: employer-plan special enrollment request generally within 30 days of marriage or adding a child; Marketplace is distinct.

sources.name: HealthCare.gov: special enrollment opportunities
sources.note: Full page opened: 60-day household-event windows and conditions; divorce without loss of coverage does not qualify on that basis.

what-happens-to-your-pets-if-something-h.title: Who will care for your pets if you cannot?
what-happens-to-your-pets-if-something-h.dek: Arrange an immediate pet caregiver, a longer-term backup and usable care instructions, then check how authority and funding would work.
what-happens-to-your-pets-if-something-h.metaDescription: Arrange an immediate pet caregiver, a longer-term backup and usable care instructions, then check how authority and funding would work.

paragraphs: Arrange a willing person who can reach your pets immediately, a backup, and someone prepared for longer-term care if you cannot return. Give them current care information, a vet contact and an agreed way to cover costs. A name in a will or a note in a drawer does not ensure that an animal will be fed tonight.

The person who can visit this evening may not be able to adopt an animal permanently. Separating those jobs makes the plan more realistic. This guide focuses on practical US emergency and estate preparation. It does not draft a trust, choose veterinary treatment or establish anyone's legal authority.

body.heading: Make the first-day plan usable
items: Ask an immediate caregiver and a backup, explaining the animals, location and likely tasks rather than simply asking for a general favor.
Arrange permitted home access and test it. Identify where carriers, leads, food and current veterinary instructions are kept.
Create a record for each animal: identifying details, routine, behavior, vet and relevant care documents. Date it.
Discuss emergency veterinary contact, consent and payment arrangements directly with the clinic. Do not assume the clinic can discuss or charge everything to anyone who calls.
Ask a longer-term caregiver separately and discuss housing, other animals, costs and whether animals should remain together.
Keep an accessible alert and contact plan so someone knows pets are at home. Share the necessary information with the agreed caregivers.

paragraphs: [Open the free pet emergency and longer-term care plan](/guides/print/library/what-happens-to-your-pets-if-something-happens-to-you.html). Use the worksheet without an account or purchase.

body.alt: Pet-care stages distinguish immediate visits, ongoing help, permanent placement and supporting authority and funds.
body.caption: One person can hold several roles, but agreement is needed for each.

body.heading: One animal, three arrangements
rows: Who can enter and provide immediate care.
Agreed name, backup and permitted access route.
Who can cover a longer absence or take the animal.
Who can approve relevant care and pay.

body.heading: Example: the neighbor and the permanent caregiver
paragraphs: Invented example: Alex's neighbor agrees to check on a cat during an unexpected hospital stay. A sibling living farther away is willing to provide longer-term care. The neighbor knows where food and the carrier are, and both people have the vet contact and current instruction location. They discuss what happens if the sibling cannot travel promptly.

The record does not say "give the usual pill" or supply a dose invented for this example. Any medication instruction is copied from the current veterinary plan and checked with the clinic where necessary. A change in health or prescription triggers an update of the care record, not a handwritten guess by a helper.

body.heading: Write instructions another person can follow
paragraphs: Include the actual food and feeding routine, safe handling, escape risks, compatibility with other animals and any transport concerns. A photograph and identifying information can help distinguish animals in a multi-pet home. Keep registration, microchip and insurance details in an appropriately protected place.

Distinguish a normal preference from a safety issue. "Hides behind the sofa when visitors arrive" is useful for finding an animal; "must remain indoors" needs to be prominent. Avoid a long biography that buries the immediate tasks. Ask the caregiver to locate supplies during a practice visit if practical.

body.heading: A written plan and a legal plan do different work
paragraphs: The [ASPCA planning guide](https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/pet-planning/making-plan-your-pet) recommends separate emergency and longer-term caregivers and a pet portfolio. It also explains that wills can take time to administer, so an informal practical arrangement remains important even when estate planning exists.

A letter of wishes can describe care but is not automatically an enforceable funding arrangement. A will provision, lifetime authority or pet trust may address different needs. Do not assume every owner needs the same structure or that a healthy animal makes formal planning unnecessary.

body.alt: Four parts of an animal-care handoff cover identity, routine, current veterinary instructions and an agreed backup.
body.caption: Keep veterinary instructions current; do not improvise them.

body.heading: Ask how costs will actually be covered
paragraphs: Estimate ordinary and known ongoing costs from real records, then discuss who would pay in a short emergency and how funds would reach a longer-term caregiver. Do not promise an inheritance can be used immediately. Ask an adviser what arrangement fits your jurisdiction and intended timing.

The [ASPCA trust primer](https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/pet-planning/pet-trust-primer) describes a trust with a trustee, caregiver, successors and funding provisions; some arrangements may address incapacity during life. It is an overview, not verification of your state's law or a do-it-yourself legal document. Complicated care, long-lived species or a desire for enforceable oversight are reasons to seek specific advice.

body.heading: Ask a caregiver and the clinic

items.line: Could you provide immediate care if I were unexpectedly away? I would like to show you the supplies and current instructions, agree the limits of what you can do, and name someone else if you are unavailable.
I am planning for an absence. What authorization and payment arrangements should be in place for a named helper, and how should they obtain current care instructions if something changes?

body.heading: If nobody can commit
paragraphs: Contact suitable local welfare or species-specific organizations in advance and ask what they actually offer, whether there is an agreement and what capacity or fees apply. Do not write a rescue's name into the plan as though it has accepted the animal. For boarding, confirm duration, health requirements, payment and who can collect the animal.

If animals are currently unattended or unsafe, arrange immediate local assistance rather than waiting for legal planning. If a caregiver cannot meet an animal's needs, contact the vet or an appropriate organization promptly. A plan should make that limitation visible, not pressure someone into tasks they cannot safely perform.

body.heading: Review people as well as instructions
paragraphs: A caregiver can move, develop an allergy, change housing or become unable to help. Check willingness after major changes and periodically as an organizing habit. Keep backups informed about the role rather than leaving them to discover it in a crisis.

Remove stale instructions from the handoff record and tell the people who have copies when something important changes. The [hospital household handoff](/guides/hospital-for-two-weeks-what-would-someone-need-to-find) can link animal care with home access and other immediate responsibilities without exposing the full private file.

items.q: Is naming someone in my will enough?
items.a: Not for immediate care. A will may be part of the longer-term arrangement, but an animal needs a reachable person and practical instructions before estate administration is complete. Ask the proposed caregiver, arrange access and costs, and obtain advice on how the legal plan should support that practical arrangement.

items.q: Does the emergency caregiver have to keep the pet permanently?
items.a: No. A nearby person may cover the first days while another provides longer-term care. Discuss each role explicitly, including transport and what happens if the longer-term person cannot act. Do not assume agreeing to feed an animal occasionally means agreeing to take ownership.

items.q: Should I create a pet trust?
items.a: That depends on the needs, costs, people involved and the law that applies. A trust may support funding and enforceable instructions, but it needs proper design and implementation. Start by identifying care and cost requirements, then ask a qualified adviser whether a trust or another arrangement serves them.

sources.name: ASPCA: making a plan for your pet
sources.note: Organization guidance returned through search: separate emergency and permanent caregivers, pet portfolio, funding, and limits of informal plans and wills.

sources.name: ASPCA: pet trust primer
sources.note: Organization guidance returned through search: trustee, successor caregiver, funding, enforcement, and possible lifetime-incapacity planning. No individual state statute verified.

what-is-due-on-my-car-right-now.title: What maintenance is due on my car right now?
what-is-due-on-my-car-right-now.dek: Use your vehicle's schedule, a fresh odometer reading and last-service evidence to identify due, upcoming and unknown maintenance without guessing.
what-is-due-on-my-car-right-now.metaDescription: Use your vehicle's schedule, a fresh odometer reading and last-service evidence to identify due, upcoming and unknown maintenance without guessing.

paragraphs: A maintenance task is due when it reaches the mileage or time limit specified for your vehicle, whichever applies first where the schedule gives both. Compare the current reading and date with reliable last-service evidence. If that evidence is missing, mark the task unknown, not safe to postpone. Warning signs and safety concerns need assessment even when a schedule says a task is not due.

The reminder sticker, manual and shop recommendation may each describe something different. Your first job is to identify the correct vehicle schedule and the facts behind the last service, then calculate what remains. This guide explains that administrative check; it cannot diagnose the vehicle, supply universal intervals or certify that it is safe to drive.

body.heading: Work out the status one task at a time
items: Identify the exact year, model, engine or powertrain and relevant schedule. Use the manufacturer's information, including applicable driving-condition provisions.
Read the current odometer and record the date and units. Do not combine a kilometer reading with a mileage interval.
Find the last-service date, odometer and task description on the receipt, your record or the servicing shop's evidence. Distinguish inspection from replacement.
Copy the actual applicable interval or manufacturer service-life instruction. Some systems use a monitor rather than a simple repeated arithmetic interval.
Calculate mileage and date thresholds where the schedule provides them. Reaching either applicable limit makes the task due; both do not have to be reached.
Separate due, upcoming and unknown tasks, then discuss uncertainty or symptoms with a qualified mechanic. Save the completed work and evidence for the next check.

paragraphs: [Open the free maintenance due and unknown-history check](/guides/print/library/what-is-due-on-my-car-right-now.html). Use the worksheet without an account or purchase.

body.alt: Four maintenance states distinguish mileage due, time due, upcoming and unknown history.
body.caption: Use the vehicle's actual instructions; the worked numbers are not recommendations.

body.heading: Example: one car on November 17, 2026 at 52,300 miles
rows: Due by time, even with 800 miles remaining.
100 miles remaining under this example interval.
2,700 miles and the stated date remain.
Unknown; ask about assessment and the correct schedule.

body.heading: The table is arithmetic, not a service schedule
paragraphs: Every interval and service record in the table is invented. Do not copy these numbers to your car. The oil example is already due by the date limit even though mileage remains. The cabin-filter example gives both remaining thresholds; it does not predict which will arrive first without knowing future use.

Add the mileage interval to the last recorded mileage to find the next mileage threshold. Add the applicable calendar interval to the actual last-service date to find the date threshold, following the manufacturer's instructions. For one-limit tasks, use the specified limit rather than inventing a second one.

body.heading: The manufacturer schedule is the starting point
paragraphs: The [FTC auto-repair guide](https://www.bulkorder.ftc.gov/system/files/publications/pdf-0078-auto-repair.pdf) recommends following the manufacturer's maintenance schedule for your type of driving. Confirm which conditions and schedule apply to the exact vehicle. Do not automatically shorten every interval because one journey was dusty or assume a generic normal schedule covers sustained demanding use.

If a shop recommends earlier work, ask whether it is based on a schedule, an observed condition, a diagnostic result or shop policy. Those can all be different from a factory interval. Record the explanation and proposed work before authorization. An inspection finding may require action even when the scheduled replacement point has not arrived.

body.alt: Four record components connect the manufacturer schedule, last service, current reading and completed-work evidence.
body.caption: A tracker cannot establish facts that were never entered or verified.

body.heading: Unknown is not the same as not due
paragraphs: A missing receipt does not prove work was never performed, but it also does not establish that the task can wait. Ask prior shops or the seller for records and keep estimates clearly labelled as unverified. Do not reset a service clock to today just because today is when you began using a tracker.

For unknown safety-critical maintenance, ask a qualified mechanic how to establish an appropriate baseline now. Some tasks cannot be verified merely by looking at the component. Keep the distinction between history recovered, condition assessed and work actually completed. The [used-car records guide](/guides/used-car-no-service-records-what-to-do) addresses that broader history problem.

body.heading: Ask why work is recommended

items.line: Is this task due under the manufacturer schedule for this vehicle and driving, or are you recommending it because of a specific finding? Please show me the interval or explain the finding and the consequence of waiting.
I do not have reliable evidence of the last service. What can you establish, what remains unknown and what baseline work or inspection do you recommend before I rely on the vehicle?

body.heading: Do not calculate past a warning sign
paragraphs: A date comparison is not a diagnosis. A warning light, leak, braking or steering concern, overheating, unusual vibration or other safety issue needs the response described by the owner's manual and appropriate professional help. Do not continue driving merely because the maintenance table looks green.

For tire pressure, [NHTSA](https://www.nhtsa.gov/summer-driving-tips) points to the vehicle placard or manual, checked cold, not the maximum marked on the tire. That is a separate practical check, not something the last oil receipt settles. If the vehicle may be unsafe, arrange assistance rather than driving it to meet an appointment.

body.heading: Keep the next check auditable
paragraphs: After work, record the date, odometer, exact task and receipt location. Note whether an item was inspected, adjusted or replaced. Refresh the current reading before another due check or a long trip; stale mileage can make an apparently upcoming task already due.

[Vehicle Maintenance Companion](/shop/vehicle-maintenance-companion) can organize entered intervals and history, but its published listing does not claim live vehicle data or a factory schedule lookup. Whatever tool you choose, the schedule and evidence you enter determine the usefulness of the result.

items.q: Is service due only when both miles and months pass?
items.a: No. Where the manufacturer specifies either limit, reaching either one makes the task due. A low-mileage vehicle can reach a time limit first. If the manufacturer provides only one limit or uses a service-life system, follow that instruction rather than forcing it into a two-number template.

items.q: Can an unknown task be overdue?
items.a: It may be, but missing history prevents a reliable scheduled comparison. Mark it unknown and seek records or professional advice rather than calling it not due. Do not wait indefinitely for a future service to create a baseline where a safety-critical task needs assessment now.

items.q: Should I use the shop's interval or the manual?
items.a: Start with the correct manufacturer schedule and ask why the shop recommends a different action. A specific condition or diagnostic finding may matter independently of routine timing. Keep the schedule, finding and authorization distinct, and get another qualified opinion where the explanation is unclear or consequential.

sources.name: FTC: auto repair basics
sources.note: Official PDF search text: follow manufacturer maintenance schedule for the type of driving. No vehicle-specific service intervals verified.

sources.name: NHTSA: summer driving and road trip tips
sources.note: Official text returned through search: use vehicle placard for cold tire pressure, inspect spare, allow rest and driver changes. Not a universal daily driving limit.

who-to-tell-when-someone-dies.title: Who to notify when someone dies: a working list
who-to-tell-when-someone-dies.dek: Prioritize death notifications by benefits, immediate risks and account needs, then track requirements without treating suggested timing as law.
who-to-tell-when-someone-dies.metaDescription: Prioritize death notifications by benefits, immediate risks and account needs, then track requirements without treating suggested timing as law.

paragraphs: After a death, first notify the people needed for immediate care and practical arrangements, confirm Social Security reporting where relevant, and identify benefits, insurance or household services that need prompt attention. Then work through institutions using a notification log. There is no universal rule that every bank or utility can safely wait a week.

The same news has to be repeated to people who ask different questions. A short record of whom you contacted, what they require and what happens next can prevent repeated calls. This guide focuses on US notifications, not the full probate process. Local deadlines and the person's circumstances may change the order.

body.heading: Start with a manageable notification pass
items: Tell close family and the people responsible for children, dependents, animals or an unattended home. Delegate personal messages if helpful.
Ask the funeral director whether the death has been reported to Social Security, if relevant. Record who is reporting and what remains to be done.
Identify active benefits, pension, employer and insurance contacts. Ask about ongoing payments, survivor options and any deadlines that apply.
Contact financial institutions through verified channels. Ask what a notification does to access and what evidence is required for the next action.
Preserve essential household services while asking about transfer or closure. Do not cancel every payment or service indiscriminately.
Keep a dated log of requests, reference numbers, documents sent, response dates and the authorized person handling each task.

paragraphs: [Open the free death notification and follow-up log](/guides/print/library/who-to-tell-when-someone-dies.html). Use the worksheet without an account or purchase.

body.alt: Four notification states distinguish reporting a death from documents, authorized action and completion confirmation.
body.caption: A completed phone call may leave several administrative steps open.

body.heading: Who belongs on the working list
rows: Stop or correct benefits and ask about survivor processes.
Has a report already been made, and which payments need review?
Pay, benefits, pension and possible dependent coverage changes.
Who handles bereavement administration and deadlines?
Protect accounts and establish the next authorized process.
What does notification change, and what documents are needed?
Claims and continuity of property or other necessary cover.
What notice and evidence does the policy require?
What is the current reporting procedure and how is it confirmed?
Transfer, preserve or close services as appropriate.
Will closure affect residents, security or other accounts?
Final filings, identification and ownership procedures.
Which process applies and who may complete it?

body.heading: Verify the government notification chain
paragraphs: [USAGov](https://www.usa.gov/report-a-death?_hsmi=330340981) says the funeral director should report the death to SSA; if that does not happen, it should be reported promptly. SSA notifies Medicare. Other benefit programs can need separate contact. Record the actual reporting status instead of assuming every agency is informed by one death certificate.

Do not spend or return a benefit deposit based only on the date it arrived. Ask the payer which benefit period it covers and what repayment or correction procedure applies. Notification is also an opportunity to ask about survivor benefits, but eligibility and applications are separate from stopping the deceased person's payment.

body.heading: Example: the order changes with the household
paragraphs: Invented example: a daughter is helping after her father dies. She confirms that the funeral director will handle SSA reporting, then prioritizes his employer because her mother's health coverage may be affected. She also calls the home insurer because the house will be unoccupied. A seldom-used club membership waits while those questions are resolved.

Her log distinguishes "death reported" from "claim submitted" and "account closed." When a provider asks for authority documents she does not yet have, she records the request and refers it to the person handling the estate. She does not represent herself as executor solely because the will names her.

body.alt: A risk-based notification sequence covers care, benefits, financial providers and household services.
body.caption: A policy deadline or immediate risk can change the order.

body.heading: Use one factual opening

items.line: I am reporting the death of the account holder. Please explain your bereavement process, what happens to the service or account now, and what evidence the authorized representative needs for the next step.
Could you let these people know and tell them who to contact about arrangements? Please do not share private financial details or forward documents.

body.heading: Notification is not permission to close or transfer
paragraphs: A family member may be able to report a death without having authority to transact, distribute property or sign closure instructions. Ask each institution to distinguish those steps. Joint ownership, beneficiary claims and estate assets may follow different processes. Do not use the deceased person's online identity to make changes as if they were still acting.

Before shutting a phone number or email service, consider how remaining account recovery and correspondence will be handled through permitted provider processes. That is not a reason to bypass access rules. Similarly, keep water, heating or security services appropriate for any occupied or vulnerable property until the responsible person agrees the next step.

body.heading: Documents: ask before ordering or sending
paragraphs: There is no universally correct number of certified death certificates to order. List institutions, ask what evidence they need, whether a certified copy is returned and whether a permitted alternative works. Keep copies and dispatch records where appropriate. Do not send an irreplaceable original document without understanding the process.

Use official portals, verified postal addresses or numbers taken independently from statements and provider websites. A caller who knows the deceased person's name is not thereby legitimate. Limit the personal details in obituaries and broadly shared messages, and avoid sending identity documents in an unverified reply.

body.heading: Stop when the request becomes a liability question
paragraphs: The [FTC](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/debts-and-deceased-relatives?mod=article_inline) explains that relatives usually do not pay a deceased person's debts from their own funds, but exceptions exist. Do not promise personal payment because a collector is insistent. Ask for written information and direct estate matters to the authorized representative.

Get qualified help for a shutoff threat, disputed debt, unclear authority, benefits overpayment, an unoccupied property risk or a deadline notice. Do not let a suggested ordering list override a real notice with a response date. Keep that document and obtain advice specific to the situation.

items.q: Do I need to tell every government agency separately?
items.a: Not necessarily, but do not assume a single report reaches every program. Confirm SSA reporting and identify each other benefit or public service the person used. USAGov provides a useful starting list. Keep the reporting status and any separate application or repayment request distinct in your notes.

items.q: Should I close all accounts immediately?
items.a: No blanket closure rule is appropriate. Ask what notification changes and what the authorized representative should do next. Some accounts support an occupied home or another person's needs. Closing, transferring and making a beneficiary claim are different actions and may require different evidence.

items.q: How many death certificates should I order?
items.a: Build the institution list and ask what each one currently requires before choosing a number. Some need certified copies and others may use different verification. Note whether documents are returned. A fixed national recommendation can cause unnecessary cost or still leave you short for your actual circumstances.

sources.note: Official page text returned through search: funeral director reporting to SSA, Medicare notification, benefits agencies, financial institutions, and final tax return.
